newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says Germany will meet EMU goals this year.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says Germany will meet EMU goals this year.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Friday that Germany would meet Maastricht Treaty budget deficit goals this year, and that there was no talk in the government about delaying European monetary union (EMU).

"We will reach the deficit criteria," Waigel said, adding that his Christian Social Union party's position was clear that this means reaching a budget deficit ratio of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.
Waigel said Germany would do everything possible to meet this goal, stating again the government would take additional measures to ensure the country's finances would be in order for currency union.

Waigel declined to give more details on Bonn's fund raising plans, saying only the government would continue to privatise companies and that any extraordinary spending would have to be approved personally by him.
Asked whether a tax hike might be considered, Waigel said: "A rise in indirect taxes for 1997 is hardly possible anymore."
Speaking at a news conference, Waigel said the government's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP) did not want indirect tax hikes.
Pressed further, Waigel said he would only present a budget that would be constitutionally viable, but added: "As finance minister I can rule nothing out."
The government has said it plans to pare its stake in telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom AG.
Waigel said: "We are sure we will come to a positive solution," on the Telekom issue.
He added: "We are currently thinking about how to reduce our stake," stressing that small shareholder interests would not be compromised in this process.

Asked about progress on finding a solution to the dispute with the Bundesbank over revaluation of its assets, Waigel declared: "I can only say that I see a good chance for a mutually beneficial solution, as (Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm) Gaddum has said today."

Waigel said that it would be dangerous for any senior government official to talk about delaying monetary union beyond its planned launch in January 1999. "If we were to discuss a delay, I would have a reaction on the markets on Monday that would harm the German and Bavarian export industries," he said.
